surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (Europe)
surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A business-to-consumer (B2C) market research questionnaire about Running Shoes. Every question asks about Running Shoes specifically — not the wider market, not adjacent categories, and not any named brand. It is designed to tell a client what buyers in Europe actually do and want in this category.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Europe who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults who have bought running shoes for themselves in the past 12 months; Adults who run or jog regularly (at least once a week) and intend to buy running shoes in the next 6 months; Adults who consider running shoes as their primary athletic footwear for exercise. Excluded: Children under 18 (unless buying for themselves, but typically parent proxy); Professional athletes or elite runners (niche, not representative of mass market); Institutional buyers (e.g., gyms, schools, military) – not consumer segment; People who only buy running shoes for fashion without any running activity.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Running shoes are purchased by individual consumers for personal athletic and casual use. While some running shoes are sold to institutions (e.g., for team sports), the dominant market is everyday consumers buying for themselves.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least once a week
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness or casual wear
Researches product reviews and compares brands before buying
Values performance features (cushioning, support, weight) and brand reputation
May participate in running events or use fitness apps
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income — these define who was recruited, not what is measured, so they appear in the audience definition rather than as questions.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running — how often, where, and why they run — to segment the audience. It then moves into the purchase journey, from what triggers a new shoe purchase, through research and channel choice, to replacement cycle, spend, and decision factors. Next, it explores product expectations, starting with must-have features, fit and sizing, quality cues, and sustainability, then trade-offs and value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, recommendation intent, and future running plans, ending on a forward-loo

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in Europe — who Adults who have bought running shoes for themselves in the past 12 months; Adults who run or jog regularly (at least once a week) and intend to buy running shoes in the next 6 months; Adults who consider running shoes as their primary athletic footwear for exercise. The consumer market for running shoes is broad, spanning casual joggers to serious amateurs. The audience is defined by personal use and purchase, with a focus on regular runners who are likely to have recent purchase intent. Excluding professional athletes keeps the survey representative of the mass consumer market.

Running shoes are considered a consumer good with high household penetration.
The survey targets individual buyers, not parents buying for children (unless the child is the end-user, but we focus on adult buyers).

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running — how often, where, and why they run — to segment the audience. It then moves into the purchase journey, from what triggers a new shoe purchase, through research and channel choice, to replacement cycle, spend, and decision factors. Next, it explores product expectations, starting with must-have features, fit and sizing, quality cues, and sustainability, then trade-offs and value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, recommendation intent, and future running plans, ending on a forward-loo
storyline_notes: For consumer_profile, dropped 'household_role' because running shoes are typically a personal purchase; added 'running_context' to capture the variety of running environments (road, trail, treadmill) which is crucial for shoe needs.
For buying_behavior, added 'replacement_cycle' instead of generic 'purchase_cycle' to reflect the durable nature of running shoes and the importance of wear and mileage.
For preferences_expectations, added a category-specific 'fit_and_sizing' beat because fit is a top pain point and a key differentiator in footwear; this has no canonical equivalent.
For preferences_expectations, emphasized 'sustainability_claims' given Europe's strong environmental awareness, and placed it before trade-offs to keep the flow from concrete to abstract.
For satisfaction_future_intent, kept the canonical order but renamed beats to be running-specific, and placed 'recommend_intent' before 'future_running_plans' to end on a forward-looking note.
Throughout, ensured no brand names are mentioned and that money-related questions (spend, value) are placed late in their sections.
